Rhubarb stalks lean
toward the fence—the wind carries
a neighbour's laughter

Tomato vines heavy,
a bumblebee naps in shade
below the south wall

Morning dew on mint,
a robin's polite inspection,
then gone, just the leaves

Wisteria spills
over the old shed roof—
who is keeping time?

First frost on the kale,
a fox pauses in the path,
finds nothing worth theft

The compost heap steams
softly in January dusk—
decomposing light

Snap peas climbing up
the trellis—they do not ask
where this is going

Strawberry runners
reach for the garden's edge,
little arms outstretched

The greenhouse glass sweats
in April's uncertain sun—
somewhere, tomatoes

Earthworms in the dark,
small citizens of the rain,
surfacing, startled

Sunflowers bow heavy,
the bees have had enough—
afternoon slows down

Basil in a cracked
clay pot on the sill, winter
is not ready yet

Dahlias like fists
opening, opening, opening,
into the cold air

A sparrow hops through
the silent Tuesday garden—
no one's watching, but

Lavender releases
its scent into the evening
without being asked

The first courgette swells
under a ruffled green leaf—
discovery, always

A snail traverses
the garden path with patience—
time is a flat thing

Pumpkin tendrils curl
as if remembering something—
the fence, maybe

Ivy takes the wall
stone by stone—not hurrying,
not stopping either

Mushrooms after rain,
little parasols arriving
for a party of one

Apple blossom falls
on the kitchen-garden path—
the bees collect it

A ladybug rests
on the rim of an old can—
everything is enough

Hydrangeas turn blue
or pink, by the soil's chemistry—
unfixed, still lovely

The shed smells of last
year's tomato leaves—nothing
in a garden is wasted

Bluebells in April
where no one is listening—
as always, enough

A cabbage white drifts
past the allotment fence—
purposeless, perfect

The robin returns
to the same patch of turned earth—
memory in wings

Wood-pigeon coos
from the old apple tree's shade—
afternoon unzips

The scarecrow's straw hat
tilts toward the autumn field—
nothing left to guard

A hedgehog rustles
through the bramble at dusk—
polite neighbour

Frost etches a leaf
in geometries of cold—
art no one signs

The pond's quiet eye
reflects a drifting magpie—
look, this is looking

Nasturtiums riot
around the potato bed—
orange cannot lie

A pear ripens silent
for three days, then falls—
no witness, no problem

Crocuses emerge
through the last skin of old snow—
brave little heresies

The greenhouse door swings
in a warm June wind—inside,
the tomatoes breathe

A wren investigates
the compost bin's interior—
tiny surveyor

Forget-me-nots spread
in the shade of the pear tree—
forgetting is easier

An old watering can
clangs against the brick wall—
startled blackbird

Raspberry canes drip
scarlet over the fence line—
small thefts forgiven

The moon rises over
a garden quiet with sleep—
moles work the night shift

A cabbage considers
a cabbage across the row—
long conversations

Foxgloves lean into
the hedge they grew up with—
old friendships, steady

Onions cure by the
kitchen door—paper skins
catch the last warm sun

Beetroots swell quietly
under the mulch of old leaves—
red secrets kept

A heron stands still
at the pond's edge—the koi
pretend to be stones

Plum trees drop their fruit
onto the long grass, too tired
to hold them longer

Spiderweb in the
rosemary bush at dawn, wet—
a geometry lesson

The seed tray on the sill
holds nothing visible yet—
patience is a crop

A mole's new tunnel
creases the lawn overnight—
breakfast will be worms

Rosemary releases
scent as the cat walks through—
afternoon rearranged

Crab-apple confetti
scatters across the cold path—
October parade

A swallow threads the
air above the greenhouse—thread
pulled through spring's fabric

The cat dreams in the
wheelbarrow while the sparrows
plan their small careers

Echinacea goes
to seed—the goldfinches come
to audit the harvest

Holly berries redden
before the first snow settles—
readiness, quiet

Moss softens the stone
step at the shed door—
time makes things gentler

Asparagus spears
rise at dawn—old promises
kept without mention

A toad sits very still
in the shade of the rhubarb—
ancient job, done well

Pear tree in blossom,
the allotment briefly church—
bees, congregation

The hose leaks slowly
into the tomato bed—
also a rhythm

Magnolia petals
line the garden path like hands—
walking through applause

A bee lands on the
forget-me-nots and disappears
into the blue

Swiss chard in winter
glows improbably red—the
garden's small defiance

Three onions forgotten
in the summer bed—now green
towers, swaying

The beech hedge holds its
copper leaves through January—
stubborn, or sleeping

The first daffodil
opens on a Tuesday morning—
Tuesday is changed

A thrush cracks a snail
on the path stone—dinner bell
of the morning garden

Hellebores nod low
under heavy February snow—
old stoics, blooming

The bean tepee tilts
in November's first real wind—
harvest was enough

A kestrel stalls high
above the allotment—long
noon, longer silence

Quince in the hedge,
lantern-yellow, uncollected—
someone will, soon

The leek's blue-green stem
straightens after rain like it
heard good news finally

Dandelion seeds
embark from the old stone wall—
a fleet, without maps

Rose hips red against
November's cold grey sky—small
flags of patience, flown

A green frog settles
into the old watering can—
new address, fine with it

Mist rolls through the
orchard at dawn—apples dream
of becoming other things

A rabbit enters
the garden with an opinion—
the lettuce listens

The pumpkin turns orange
while nobody is watching—
private ceremony

Aphids on the roses,
the ladybugs in slow pursuit—
ancient bureaucracy

Tulips in April
lean all the same direction—
a polite agreement

A green woodpecker
works the old lawn methodically—
ants, small surprises

Freshly turned earth
smells like nothing else—winter
softening its grip

The bramble takes the
fence a millimetre a day—
no one is alarmed

Elderflower sprays
hang low over the path—heavy
with next year's cordial

A dragonfly skims
the pond's brown water—summer
held in a wingbeat

The quince ripens slow,
yellow, taking all the time
it can get, rightly

Carrots still warm from
August afternoon in the earth—
sweet with small dirt

Moths gather dusk-thick
around the hedgerow gate lamp—
nobody is out

A hen pecks the cold
December ground—patient,
the world will give

Bean flowers, white and
scarlet, shiver in June's first
proper warm wind

A blackbird sings the
same phrase every dawn this week—
it means something, probably

The garden after
rain has the look of something
loved—shine everywhere

The greenhouse tomatoes
crack in August heat—forgave them
nothing, asked nothing

A fox saunters past
at midnight—the garden holds
its breath, politely

Lilac branch indoors
perfumes the cold kitchen—April
brought inside, held close

Butterflies on the
buddleia bush all afternoon—
the fence keeps nothing out

Teasels hold their dry
purple crowns against the sleet—
last year's persistence

The owl calls once
from the edge of the garden—
night, briefly visible

First light finds the
garden soft with yesterday's rain—
nothing has left, yet
